output.reason: This lens compares the 18 supplied NL contracts against the exact source inventory and closed FCSTM/inspection facts to find omitted/collapsed contracts, containment/entry defects, transition-group collisions, wrong local-exit targets, and unauthorized edges. Key finding: the source and model merge 'Accelerating' and 'Cruising' into one single state 'AcceleratingOrCruising', so all NL contracts that treat Accelerating and Cruising as two distinct substates/endpoints are structurally collapsed against the closed model. The root scope's initial entry into Operate is realized only indirectly through Off (start signal); Operate's owner-local entry into Idle is a plain unconditional edge (satisfied). Also, the keyOff exit pattern (Operate -> Off transition guarded by a route-token variable set by inner keyOff transitions to [*]) creates a wrong-target/collapsed structural issue for NL2-ENDPOINT-OFF (direct keyOff transition expected but actual model routes the trigger and the target-reaching transition across two separate closed transitions). I evaluate containment contracts as satisfied (Idle, AcceleratingOrCruising, Braking are all direct children of Operate; Accelerating and Cruising map to the same single state, so containment holds for that merged identity but the separate labeled containment contracts for Accelerating and Cruising both resolve to the same one state, which is a structural collapse, not a missing containment). I focus my candidates on defects visible from contract-structure comparison: (1) the transition-group/endpoint contract for Idle->Accelerating maps onto a shared merged-target edge (structural collision with the Cruising alternative), (2) the transition-group/endpoint contract for Idle->Cruising maps onto the same shared edge (its own independent candidate, kept single-target per contract), (3) the derived guard_disjointness contract for Accelerating/Cruising indistinguishability is strongly supported since they are literally the same closed state, and (4) NL2-ENDPOINT-OFF's expected direct keyOff edge out of Operate exists structurally only as a guarded/effect-mediated transition depending on an internal route token rather than one authored keyOff-triggered edge to Off, which is a wrong-target/trigger-mismatch worth flagging. I split the derived additional contract into two single-target endpoint contracts (one for Accelerating, one for Cruising) to satisfy the at-most-one-target-per-contract structural rule, keeping each independently violable, and added the required scope field to each.

arguments.reason: This lens compares the 18 supplied NL contracts against the exact source inventory and closed FCSTM/inspection facts to find omitted/collapsed contracts, containment/entry defects, transition-group collisions, wrong local-exit targets, and unauthorized edges. Key finding: the source and model merge 'Accelerating' and 'Cruising' into one single state 'AcceleratingOrCruising', so all NL contracts that treat Accelerating and Cruising as two distinct substates/endpoints are structurally collapsed against the closed model. The root scope's initial entry into Operate is realized only indirectly through Off (start signal); Operate's owner-local entry into Idle is a plain unconditional edge (satisfied). Also, the keyOff exit pattern (Operate -> Off transition guarded by a route-token variable set by inner keyOff transitions to [*]) creates a wrong-target/collapsed structural issue for NL2-ENDPOINT-OFF (direct keyOff transition expected but actual model routes the trigger and the target-reaching transition across two separate closed transitions). I evaluate containment contracts as satisfied (Idle, AcceleratingOrCruising, Braking are all direct children of Operate; Accelerating and Cruising map to the same single state, so containment holds for that merged identity but the separate labeled containment contracts for Accelerating and Cruising both resolve to the same one state, which is a structural collapse, not a missing containment). I focus my candidates on defects visible from contract-structure comparison: (1) the transition-group/endpoint contract for Idle->Accelerating maps onto a shared merged-target edge (structural collision with the Cruising alternative), (2) the transition-group/endpoint contract for Idle->Cruising maps onto the same shared edge (its own independent candidate, kept single-target per contract), (3) the derived guard_disjointness contract for Accelerating/Cruising indistinguishability is strongly supported since they are literally the same closed state, and (4) NL2-ENDPOINT-OFF's expected direct keyOff edge out of Operate exists structurally only as a guarded/effect-mediated transition depending on an internal route token rather than one authored keyOff-triggered edge to Off, which is a wrong-target/trigger-mismatch worth flagging. I split the derived additional contract into two single-target endpoint contracts (one for Accelerating, one for Cruising) to satisfy the at-most-one-target-per-contract structural rule, keeping each independently violable, and added the required scope field to each.

branches.reason: This lens compares the 18 supplied NL contracts against the exact source inventory and closed FCSTM/inspection facts to find omitted/collapsed contracts, containment/entry defects, transition-group collisions, wrong local-exit targets, and unauthorized edges. Key finding: the source and model merge 'Accelerating' and 'Cruising' into one single state 'AcceleratingOrCruising', so all NL contracts that treat Accelerating and Cruising as two distinct substates/endpoints are structurally collapsed against the closed model. The root scope's initial entry into Operate is realized only indirectly through Off (start signal); Operate's owner-local entry into Idle is a plain unconditional edge (satisfied). Also, the keyOff exit pattern (Operate -> Off transition guarded by a route-token variable set by inner keyOff transitions to [*]) creates a wrong-target/collapsed structural issue for NL2-ENDPOINT-OFF (direct keyOff transition expected but actual model routes the trigger and the target-reaching transition across two separate closed transitions). I evaluate containment contracts as satisfied (Idle, AcceleratingOrCruising, Braking are all direct children of Operate; Accelerating and Cruising map to the same single state, so containment holds for that merged identity but the separate labeled containment contracts for Accelerating and Cruising both resolve to the same one state, which is a structural collapse, not a missing containment). I focus my candidates on defects visible from contract-structure comparison: (1) the transition-group/endpoint contract for Idle->Accelerating maps onto a shared merged-target edge (structural collision with the Cruising alternative), (2) the transition-group/endpoint contract for Idle->Cruising maps onto the same shared edge (its own independent candidate, kept single-target per contract), (3) the derived guard_disjointness contract for Accelerating/Cruising indistinguishability is strongly supported since they are literally the same closed state, and (4) NL2-ENDPOINT-OFF's expected direct keyOff edge out of Operate exists structurally only as a guarded/effect-mediated transition depending on an internal route token rather than one authored keyOff-triggered edge to Off, which is a wrong-target/trigger-mismatch worth flagging. I split the derived additional contract into two single-target endpoint contracts (one for Accelerating, one for Cruising) to satisfy the at-most-one-target-per-contract structural rule, keeping each independently violable, and added the required scope field to each.
